stories.headline: Alaska Senate Candidate Mary Peltola and Family Hurt in Anchorage Car Crash
stories.summary:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Alaska's lone U.S. Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a three-vehicle crash in Anchorage on Saturday, her campaign said in a statement Sunday. The family was traveling to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle struck the car carrying them.

Anchorage police confirmed the collision involved three vehicles and said those involved sustained injuries described as non-life-threatening. Peltola's campaign said she would reschedule planned campaign events in Fairbanks and Bethel as a result of the accident.

The crash comes about two weeks before the midterm elections, in a race that has drawn national attention. The campaign did not immediately announce new dates for the postponed stops, and no information was provided on the cause of the collision or whether any citations were issued.

stories.headline: Italy's Salvini Re-elected League Leader After Pledging to Push Government to End Ukraine Support
stories.summary:
Matteo Salvini, an ally of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, was reelected leader of the far-right League party after promising to press the Italian government to stop supporting Ukraine. The League is part of Italy's ruling coalition.

The renewed mandate gives Salvini a platform to push a position that diverges from the government's stated backing for Kyiv. How far that pressure translates into policy within the coalition remains unclear, as Meloni has been a prominent supporter of Ukraine within European institutions.

The outcome is notable for European unity on Ukraine aid at a time when the war continues to strain political debates across the continent. Further details on coalition reaction were not immediately available.

stories.headline: UAE's Lana Nusseibeh Pledges Dialogue With Iran If Elected UN Secretary-General
stories.summary:
United Arab Emirates Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh, a candidate to become the next United Nations secretary-general, said she would pursue dialogue with Iran if selected. She cast diplomacy as a route out of the turmoil that has engulfed the Middle East.

The pledge comes as the region is gripped by conflict involving Iran, including attacks affecting Gulf states and shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Her candidacy places a Gulf diplomat at the center of the race to lead the world body.

The selection of a secretary-general involves the Security Council and General Assembly, and candidates are expected to continue outlining their platforms in the coming months.

stories.headline: Israelis Weigh Leadership Change as Pivotal General Election Nears
stories.summary:
Israel is holding a general election this week after years of war, and many Israelis regard it as the most consequential vote in decades. The country has been shaken by the October 7, 2023 attacks and the prolonged conflicts that followed.

NPR examined whether shifts in Israeli public attitudes since the attacks will translate into a change in national leadership, including the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Voters are weighing security, the conduct of the wars, and the country's direction.

The vote takes place amid West Bank movement restrictions and escalating regional tensions, including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Results are expected to shape Israel's approach to the ongoing conflict with Iran and its neighbors.

stories.headline: Update: Death Toll in Nigerian Village Raided by Gunmen Rises to 48, Police Say
stories.summary:
The death toll from Friday's attack on the remote village of Binnari in Nigeria's north-eastern Taraba state has risen to at least 48, state police told the BBC. Police had initially reported 10 deaths after unidentified gunmen on motorcycles raided the village, looting shops and setting houses ablaze. More bodies were found on Sunday, according to police spokesperson Victor Mshelizah, who said some victims drowned while trying to escape and others were killed in nearby bushes.

Amnesty International's Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, said the organisation had confirmed 52 deaths, citing sources on the ground and community members. He called for an impartial investigation and accused the authorities of leaving rural communities "at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity." The attack began just after midday Muslim prayers and continued for up to four hours.

Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told AFP the attackers arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men to each, and took cash, food and provisions as well as motorcycles abandoned by fleeing residents. Survivor Isiyaku Musa said nobody knew where it was safe to go, and another survivor said some residents remained missing. Police said the assailants had fled before officers arrived, and no casualties were reported among the gunmen.

Parts of north-eastern Nigeria have suffered years of violence involving jihadist groups and armed gangs that raid communities, abduct residents and demand ransoms, and similar groups operate in the north-west and centre of the country. The attack comes as Nigeria prepares for elections next year, with insecurity expected to feature prominently in political debate.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says It Is 'Decision Time' on Iran: Deal or 'Finish It Off'
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said it is "getting to be decision time" on whether to reach an agreement with Tehran or resume attacks, as Iranian and Houthi threats against Americans in the Middle East continue to grow. He made the remarks to reporters before boarding Air Force One, saying he is choosing between a deal and taking action to "finish them off."

Trump said there are "two very different sets of intelligence reports" on Iran, without detailing their contents. The comments come amid reports that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans to renew strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, though the White House has said no attack will occur before the vote.

The remarks follow recent U.S. intelligence warnings of Iranian plots against American officials abroad and a reduction of staffing at several Middle East embassies. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have also escalated. Analysts such as former U.S. Ambassador to Israel Daniel Shapiro have warned that another round of military operations could deepen regional and global economic strains, with oil prices already at their highest level since May.

The decision is also tied to political calendars in both countries, with elections in the United States and a pivotal vote in Israel approaching. No timeline for a decision was provided.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Fails to Change Economic Headwinds Facing GOP Candidates
stories.summary:
High gas, diesel and food prices are expected to remain elevated through Election Day, creating a strong political headwind for Republicans who are at serious risk of losing control of the House and possibly the Senate, according to The Hill. President Trump's diesel deal with Russia has had little lasting impact on fuel prices, the report said.

The outlook has put Republican candidates on the defensive in the final stretch before the midterms. Democrats have focused on cost-of-living concerns, while Republicans have pointed to administration efforts to ease energy prices, including diplomatic moves and tariff adjustments on some Canadian goods.

Separately, the Justice Department's move to try to preemptively block Alaska's Senate results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses stunned officials in both parties, the report said. Supporters of the administration have argued that election integrity concerns warrant legal preparation, while critics describe the step as unprecedented.

With roughly two weeks to go, the combination of economic pressures and election disputes is shaping the closing arguments of both parties.

stories.headline: Gabon Lifts Eight-Month Social Media Ban
stories.summary:
Gabon has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago, a move that drew widespread criticism at the time. The High Communication Authority announced the reversal on Saturday in a televised statement, and the BBC has approached the regulator for comment.

The ban was introduced on 17 February, with the authority saying online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions. It came as President Brice Oligui Nguema faced a wave of social unrest, including strikes by teachers and civil servants over low pay and poor working conditions. Many of the country's roughly 2.5 million people turned to VPNs to keep using Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram, which are popular with young people for business and leisure.

The opposition called the suspension an abuse of power. Nguema won last year's election with more than 90% of the vote, two years after a coup ended over five decades of Bongo family rule, and pledged reform, though previous governments had used digital blackouts to control information.

stories.headline: Machado Returns to Venezuela in Surprise Challenge to Acting President Rodríguez
stories.summary:
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Caracas in a surprise move on Sunday. Bloomberg reported that the return could pose the biggest test yet to acting President Delcy Rodríguez's political opening.

The move also bears on the Trump administration's strategy for post-Maduro Venezuela. Rodríguez has led the country in an acting capacity since Nicolás Maduro's departure, and has pursued a limited political opening that Machado's presence may now put under strain.

Machado has long been the most prominent figure in Venezuela's opposition. Her return raises questions about how the acting government will respond, whether she will be allowed to operate freely, and how Washington will balance its working relationship with Rodríguez against support for the opposition. Details about the circumstances of her arrival and her immediate plans were not available in the initial report.

stories.headline: Update: Early Reports Suggest Record Turnout in Serbia's Parliamentary Election
stories.summary:
Early reports indicate Serbian voters turned out in record numbers on Sunday. Preliminary figures showed 46 percent had voted by 14:00 local time, nearly a million more than at the same point in the December 2023 election. Voting ends at 20:00, with first indications of results expected about two hours later.

The high turnout is fuelling hopes for the opposition Student List, which is trying to end the rule of President Aleksandar Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party, in power since 2012. Most commentators suggest a final turnout of 65 percent or above would favour the students. The movement grew out of two years of protests after the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy that killed 16 people, widely seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence. It is campaigning on purging officials who broke rules in cracking down on protesters, keeping party loyalists out of public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster from political control.

Vucic, who cannot seek a third presidential term, is leading his party in hopes of returning as prime minister. He and the SNS deny corruption and deny seeking to influence the media. He retains strong support among voters who see him as a strong leader and credit him with economic growth and infrastructure improvements, and he has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries. Long queues formed in cities, towns and at polling stations abroad, and police closed streets around the electoral commission in Belgrade.

stories.headline: Update: Suspect's Mental State and Possible Political Motive Examined After Fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest
stories.summary:
Bavarian authorities said a 33-year-old German man detained near the Kehlsteinhaus, Adolf Hitler's Alpine retreat known as the Eagle's Nest, may have diminished responsibility. Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report found signs of possible mental illness, while a political motive is also being considered. He stressed the investigation is at an early stage.

A fire alarm sounded at 21:15 local time on Friday, and firefighters found the building engulfed. About 200 emergency personnel responded, and difficult terrain hampered efforts to control the blaze, which was still burning early Saturday. Police said the man was apprehended on a motorcycle near the scene, and nothing suggests further suspects. Local media reported the site was largely destroyed.

Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the site would under no circumstances remain a ruin, citing the importance of continuing remembrance work. Completed in 1938, the building survived 1945 and became a tourist destination with a mountain inn. Germany and Austria have debated whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish Hitler-linked buildings, with some citing historical value and others warning of neo-Nazi pilgrimage.

stories.headline: Six Flags to Install Seat Belts on Georgia Coaster After Rider's Death
stories.summary:
Six Flags Entertainment Corporation said it will add seat belts to the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, where a rider fell to his death on Oct. 12. Rides with similar restraints will receive the same upgrade. CEO John Reilly announced the step in a statement Friday, less than two weeks after the death of 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta.

Goliath remains closed while state and local officials investigate. Eight other coasters at parks in Illinois, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio and Ontario also remain shut. All nine were made by Swiss manufacturer Bolliger & Mabillard and use similar clamshell restraints. Reilly did not say which coasters will get seat belts or when the closed rides will reopen, but said independent engineers and inspectors are reviewing safety procedures across all parks.

Investigators have not said what went wrong. Witnesses said Kariem rose out of his seat and fell headfirst back into the cart before being ejected, and some earlier riders said they had concerns about the restraints. SeaWorld Orlando and La Ronde in Montreal also temporarily closed coasters with similar restraints; SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday.

stories.headline: Gunmen Kill at Least 10 Villagers, Loot Shops in Northeast Nigeria
stories.summary:
Unknown gunmen raided the remote village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area of Taraba state, northeastern Nigeria, on Friday, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police said. The attackers reportedly arrived on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers, and the rampage is said to have lasted up to four hours.

Police recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after responding to a distress call, but the attackers had fled by the time officers arrived. Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said officers were searching the nearby bush for other casualties and warned the toll could rise. Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told AFP the attackers came on about 50 motorcycles, two men to each, and took cash, food and abandoned motorcycles. Survivors counted at least 20 dead, and some residents remain missing.

Amnesty International's Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, said families of the bereaved told the group up to 50 people died, noting that the initial funeral had 37 people. He called for an impartial investigation and accused authorities of leaving rural communities "at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity."

The attack adds to a pattern of violence by armed groups across Nigeria's northwest, northeast and central regions. The country is also fighting a jihadist insurgency in the northeast that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of security.

stories.headline: Higher Energy Costs Weigh on Trump's Midterm Pitch as Obama Rallies in Michigan
stories.summary:
With the November 3 midterms about a week away, the Iran war and higher energy prices are shaping voters' economic concerns, according to analysis aired on Bloomberg. Financial Times associate editor Rana Foroohar said rising costs are a central factor as both parties push into the final stretch of early voting.

Former President Barack Obama rallied in Detroit on Saturday, the first day of early voting in Michigan, for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. He blamed inflation and high prices on President Trump, called him an agent of "chaos and cruelty," and warned of rising costs, corruption and threats to democratic values. The race could hinge on Detroit's substantial Black vote, and some undecided Black voters told reporters the endorsement had not swayed them. Republican candidate Mike Rogers, responding to Trump's description of El-Sayed as a "jihadist" and "violent terrorist," gave an interview to Meet the Press.

Trump defended his tariff policy at a Georgia rally, saying it has made the country richer, and announced that Volkswagen would build a $4.2 billion Audi plant in the state. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt described a strategy to rally Trump supporters who typically skip midterm elections and to counter weak approval ratings. A Federal Reserve report also found median family net worth rose from 2022 to 2025 for all racial and ethnic groups except Black families, whose median net worth fell 25%.

stories.headline: El Salvador's Bukele Says Bodies Handed Over in Haiti Are Not Missing Hostages
stories.summary:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said four bodies delivered to his country's special forces in Haiti are "not our men," casting doubt on whether the four missing Salvadoran air technicians have been found. He said a nongovernmental organization handed over the remains at a Haitian airport, claiming they were the missing men, but that one body was a child's and another wore a uniform from a different country's army.

Bukele posted images of a Gang Suppression Force member's ID card and a matching Chad national ID. His account contradicts a New York Times report, citing people close to the mission, that the badly burned bodies found near Port-au-Prince on Saturday were believed to be the missing men. One unnamed source told the paper the ID Bukele posted belonged to a soldier who lost it when he was injured.

The four men were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force and vanished after an ambush by heavily armed criminal groups in the Croix-des-Bouquets area. Bukele dispatched a military contingent on Thursday, reportedly about 450 soldiers, with the stated aim of returning the men alive.

Haiti has been consumed by gang violence since the 2021 assassination of its president, and the UN reported more than 5,700 people killed or injured between January 1 and September 11. The multinational force has struggled to enter areas gangs control. Identification of the remains is expected to require medical examination.

stories.headline: Trump's Former Border Patrol Chief Calls Minneapolis Withdrawal a 'Surrender'
stories.summary:
Greg Bovino, the former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the Minneapolis deportation drive, told the BBC the administration's withdrawal of agents from the city was a "surrender." Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, he said the administration "threw the towel in," that deportations were at a "virtual standstill," and that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota."

Bovino was removed from his role after the January shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti, which were captured on video and prompted a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. Trump then said he would "de-escalate a little bit" and pulled about 700 immigration agents from the state. Earlier this month Good's family filed two civil lawsuits alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with protesters' civil rights, naming Bovino and agent Jonathan Ross, who shot Good.

Bovino said he was "not responding" to the suit and that "people do lawsuits all the time." He rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined claims that Good and Pretti meant to harm agents, calling his agents the "real victims." The family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and said they look forward to deposing him. The White House has called the lawsuits "baseless."

stories.headline: Update: Israel Imposes West Bank Movement Restrictions Ahead of Pivotal Tuesday Election as Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Escalate
stories.summary:
The Israeli military announced restrictions on the movement of Palestinian workers in the run-up to Tuesday's national election. The measures follow the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen on Friday near Hebron, which prompted a full lockdown of the West Bank. Many Israelis view the vote as one of the most pivotal in the country's history, with implications beyond its borders.

Campaign coverage has focused on the ultra-Orthodox community's resistance to military conscription and whether it could bring down the Netanyahu government. Arab Israeli turnout, often depressed by disaffection, is the subject of a strong push to remove the right-wing governing coalition. More than half a million young people are also expected to vote for the first time, and could prove decisive. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has refused to take personal responsibility for the failures surrounding the October 2023 attack or to order a state inquiry.

Elsewhere in the region, the Iran-backed Houthi movement has continued strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities, with at least three deaths reported in the latest attacks at an airport and an oil field. The United Kingdom said it will provide additional defensive military support to Saudi Arabia. Yemen's army said three missiles hit a training camp in government-controlled Shabwa province on Monday.

Warnings to US officials have also intensified. The State Department has adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, and a separate attack in Jordan's southern Karak governorate left 34 people injured, with a manhunt under way.

stories.headline: Update: Almost 1,000 Arrested in French Protests as Clashes Erupt After Largely Peaceful Marches
stories.summary:
French police fired tear gas and used water cannons to disperse protesters after clashes broke out following a day of mostly peaceful demonstrations across the country. Officials said almost 1,000 people were arrested, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Authorities estimated about 410,000 people took part, while unions put the figure at roughly 800,000.

In Paris, objects were thrown at police and the demonstration turned violent. In Marseille, protesters set barricades and rubbish bins alight, and in Bordeaux demonstrators ripped boards from a shop to build a barricade. In Grenoble, hundreds of masked individuals vandalized property and attacked police with mortars and projectiles, according to officials.

Authorities appear to have avoided a repeat of the rioting and looting of 17 October, which produced some of the worst disorder in modern French history and led to more than 2,700 arrests. The government had deployed tens of thousands of officers and closed the Louvre in anticipation of unrest. President Emmanuel Macron has pledged to overhaul university admissions after meeting protesting students, though the movement has continued.

stories.headline: Update: Serbia Votes in Watershed Election as Student-Led List Challenges Vučić
stories.summary:
Serbians went to the polls in a parliamentary election that will decide whether longtime strongman Aleksandar Vučić returns as prime minister or is ousted by an unprecedented student-led opposition. The students campaign on cracking down on corruption and strengthening democracy.

The vote is widely seen as a test of Vučić's grip on power after a prolonged period of student-driven protest. Analysts describe the race as tight, with the student list the most serious challenge his camp has faced in years.

Results and any disputes over the conduct of the vote will determine whether Serbia's government changes hands or Vučić consolidates his position.

stories.headline: Twelve Injured, Including Six Children, in Shooting Near Florida A&M Stadium During Homecoming Week
stories.summary:
A shooting near Florida A&M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium in Tallahassee on Saturday night left 12 people injured, including six juveniles, police said. The shooting occurred just before 8 p.m. near Perry and Manatee streets. Eleven victims sustained gunshot wounds, and the youngest victim was 11.

One victim was in critical condition, two were seriously injured and eight were stable. Police Chief Lawrence Revell said preliminary information indicated a physical altercation involving two or three individuals preceded the gunfire, and described it as an isolated incident. No arrests had been announced.

The shooting took place during the university's Homecoming Week, when students and alumni gather for annual celebrations. Revell said officers carried victims to safety and transported them to hospitals before the scene was fully secure. The university said the campus remained safe and urged people to avoid the area while the investigation continued.
